one_liner: Keyed AES-round Rust hasher for in-memory HashMaps; about 11x faster than SipHash-1-3, claims wins over xxh3/wyhash.
what_it_does: aHash is a keyed, non-cryptographic 64-bit hash built for one job: hashing the keys of in-memory hash tables. It implements Rust's Hasher and BuildHasher traits, so it drops into std::collections::HashMap/HashSet as the hasher type parameter (HashMap<K, V, ahash::RandomState>). It also ships AHashMap/AHashSet wrappers, HashMap/HashSet type aliases, and RandomState::hash_one for one-off hashes. Each RandomState gets its own random keys (from getrandom by default), so hash values differ per map, per process, per CPU feature set and per crate version.
how_it_is_fast: When built with the aes target feature, each 16-byte block goes through one AES decryption round (aesdec) in one lane and an SSSE3 byte shuffle plus 64-bit add in a second lane. Inputs over 64 bytes are consumed 64 bytes per iteration across four independent AES lanes, and finish folds 256 bits of state to 64 with up to three AES rounds. Lengths are dispatched through a branch tree (<=8, 9-16, 17-32, 33-64, >64) that reads overlapping head and tail words instead of looping over bytes. Without AES it falls back to a 'folded multiply' (64x64->128-bit multiply, then XOR of the two halves); on nightly, min_specialization gives primitive keys a one-multiply hasher.
when_to_use: Rust HashMap/HashSet with string or byte-slice keys from about 16 bytes to a few KB, where SipHash-1-3 shows up in profiles: the project's FAQ table (i7-6700) has 1 KB strings at 25.4 ns against 254 ns for SipHash-1-3.
Maps that ingest untrusted keys (request fields, user IDs), where you want per-map random keys rather than an unkeyed hash like FxHash or FNV.

Builds where you control RUSTFLAGS and can enable -C target-feature=+aes or target-cpu=native on x86-64. The AES path is about 2x faster than the fallback on 1 KB strings (25.4 vs 54.6 ns in the FAQ table).
Integer keys with structured low bits (multiples of 1024, aligned pointers) where FxHash collapses into a few buckets.
no_std targets that still need a keyed hasher: turn off std and use compile-time-rng or explicit seeds (RandomState::with_seeds).
when_not_to_use: Anything persisted, sent over the network or compared across machines or builds. The output changes with CPU features, target-cpu flags, stable vs nightly and crate version; issue #236 was closed as intended behaviour.

Security-relevant hashing (MACs, checksums, content addressing). It is not cryptographic. A key-recovery attack using only collision checks was fixed in 0.8.4 (#163). An open report from 2026-09 (#292) shows a fixed 56-byte pair colliding for about 2^-19.4 of random keys on the AES path, against 2^-64 for an ideal keyed hash.
Default builds without the aes target feature (baseline x86-64, wasm, 32-bit targets). There is no runtime CPU detection (open #104), so these builds silently get the slower multiply fallback.

Small integer keys. FxHash is faster on u64 in aHash's own sheet (0.71 vs 0.87). foldhash's benchmark (Xeon 8481C and Apple M2, Rust 1.80.1) has foldhash ahead on most hash-table workloads (geomean 6.21 vs 8.74 ns without target-cpu=native), with aHash winning only medium-to-long strings when AES is on.
Bulk hashing of large buffers. Independent rurban SMHasher numbers (Ryzen 5 3350G) have ahash64 at 9.9 GB/s against 20.9 GB/s for xxh3 and 22.6 GB/s for wyhash.

integration.dependencies: cfg-if, zerocopy 0.8, once_cell (most targets); getrandom 0.3 through the default runtime-rng feature; optional const-random, serde, portable-atomic; build dependency version_check
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.60 declared (rust-version), but the default runtime-rng feature pulls in getrandom 0.3, which declares Rust 1.63; specialization turns on automatically on nightly
integration.platforms: Any Rust target through the fallback, including no_std. The AES path runs on x86/x86-64 and AArch64 only when compiled with the aes target feature; 32-bit ARM also needs nightly plus the nightly-arm-aes feature.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented explicitly. AHasher and RandomState are plain Clone value types with no interior mutability; global seed setup uses a once_cell OnceBox and an atomic counter, and set_random_source requires Send + Sync.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is a drop-in BuildHasher for std HashMap/HashSet in place of SipHash-1-3's RandomState. It cannot replace xxHash or wyhash as a content hash, because its output is not stable across platforms, flags or versions.

gotchas: ahash::RandomState holds four u64 keys (32 bytes), so ahash::HashMap<u32, u32> is 64 bytes against 48 for std's HashMap, according to foldhash's README.

build.rs turns on min_specialization whenever the compiler is nightly, and there is no opt-out (open #238). The same code therefore takes different paths, and gives different hash values, on stable and nightly.
The 0.8.12 patch release moved to getrandom 0.3, which broke some wasm/js builds (open #274). The workaround is to disable default features and use compile-time-rng or explicit seeds.

Users have reported slowdowns between patch releases (0.8.6 to 0.8.7, about 1.6x on an Apple M1 Pro) and with target-cpu=native on AMD Ryzen (open #194 and #190). Pin the version and benchmark on your own hardware.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick aHash over xxHash or wyhash when you are in Rust, hashing short-to-medium HashMap keys that may come from hostile input, and want per-map random keys. aHash's own page says wyhash has fixed strings that reset its state. Pick xxHash (XXH3) or wyhash when you need output that is stable across machines and versions, when you work in C/C++, or for bulk throughput, where rurban SMHasher puts both about 2x ahead of ahash64.
verified_claims_summary: The project's Criterion bench hashes a u64 and a 1 KB string through each crate's Rust BuildHasher with fat LTO; xxh3 goes through xxhash-rust's streaming Xxh3Builder. Its sheet reports aHash 0.87/19.98 against xxh3 11.88/114.14, wyhash 1.53/53.13 and SipHash-1-3 9.70/219.13, with units unlabelled (probably ns) and no rustc version or CPU stated. Independent data backs only the SipHash gap (foldhash's benchmark: 1.23 vs 9.09 ns per u64 on a Xeon 8481C with Rust 1.80.1); rurban SMHasher on a Ryzen 5 3350G puts ahash64 bulk speed at 9.9 GB/s, about half of xxh3 and wyhash.
status_note: Maintained but slow-moving: last release 0.8.12 (May 2025), last commit Nov 2025, 35 open issues including the getrandom breakage and a new collision report; dual MIT/Apache-2.0 and ubiquitous (about 790M crates.io downloads), though hashbrown replaced it with foldhash as its default hasher in 0.15.
